There are four pathophysiological factors involved in the pathogenesis [ 9 ]: Anatomical factor (obesity, craniofacial conformations of reduced dimensions, laxity of the soft palate or macroglossia, which can lead to greater collapse of the upper airways in non-obese patients, etc.) Instability of ventilatory control, also known as high loop gain Neuromuscular inefficiency of the dilator muscles of the upper airways Increased propensity for nocturnal awakenings due to respiratory stimuli, or a reduced awakening threshold, also known as low arousal threshold [ 9 ]

Increased propensity for nocturnal awakenings due to respiratory stimuli, or a reduced awakening threshold, also known as low arousal threshold [ 9 ]
